docs.text: Preface I’ve been around 8-bit computing a while. Dare I say it all has enthralled me all of my life? Maybe it was the movie Wargames (which changed my life’s trajectory for sure), or maybe the Commodore 64 I got in my teens. Regardless, I’ve been dreaming of delusions of software grandeur ever since. So much so I’ve built a career out of it. But let me let you in on a secret. I’m still average. Hell, maybe even below average. I can’t develop a kernel, or optimize some assembly code for a new disk utility. I can’t make a full game using hardware sprites or get some cool new feature to run with a device driver I built myself. I’m just a run-of-the-mill average 8-bit nerd that will never stop loving computing and will never stop trying to recreate something I loved from my childhood. Recently, after taking a hiatus from the 8-bit world, I started rekindling my excitement all over again for these new modern 8-bit systems. But the more I collected links to forums and discords, the more I noticed something about the community. The “average” user just didn’t seem to exist. Everyone was a hardware/software expert or not at all. What was that? I think it’s primarily because the systems are so new that only the elite assembly gods can work on them successfully. Either that or they simply don’t have the time or patience to bring us up to that tier. After reading a scantly slapped together manual and basking in the frustration of it, I had a small epiphany. I love the movie Tommy Boy (and that era of movies), and in it, one villain (played by Dan Ackroyd) was Zalinski of Zalinksi Auto Parts. His commercial tagline was “I make car parts for the American working-man because that’s who I am, and that’s who I care about”. The cleverness of that line resonated in that moment. I should make tutorials for the average 8-bit nerd, because that’s who I am, and that’s who I care about. So I did. This manual attempts to show more than the brief and sometimes sarcastic idioms found in most literature right now. It attempts to take things back to the Commodore 64 era of manuals. Where the examples were typed in by humble, hungry and excited 8-bit explorers who relished in the magic of home computing. It’s for those of us that want to have fun and explore what these new machines, languages and hardware can do and try to feel that feeling once again. It’s for us average people. I’m just an enthusiast like you. I’m not a subject expert of any sorts. The things I share here are things I experimented with, learned and pieced together by playing with the language. I’m just sharing the love of it. Nothing more. Nothing less. 10 print "Let’s get started!"

docs.text: Peeking and a Poking With 8-bit programming, one of the most common tasks we face is how to set specific values in memory. Even in basic we find ourselves needing to set a flag, update a color value or turn some feature on or off that just isn't reachable using the languages dialect. This is where we need to peek and poke. Lets look at a fun and simple example using the cursor and the rate that it flashes. If we look at the reference manuals for the Foenix we can see that the cursor blink rate is a set of flags inside of a memory address at $D010. Address 64 32 16 8 4 2 1 $D010 - - - Flash On/Off Flash Rate Flash Rate Enable We can look at what value is in there by default by typing: print peek ($D010) 5 The peek command will return the one-byte value of the value stored in memory address $D010. In this case its a 5. If we look at the memory information from the Foenix reference manual we can see each of the 8 bits has something to do with the cursor. The flash rate bits at 4 and 2 can be setup like this: 4 2 Total Rate 0 0 0 1s 0 1 2 1/2s 1 0 4 1/4s 1 1 6 1/5s We can change one-byte values in memory using the poke command. Let's see if we can change the cursor behaviours using the table. So when we asked what the byte was set to the system essentially told us the value 5. So The flash rate bits are set to 1 and 0 (4) and the bit 0 value is turned on (1) for a total of 5. This means if we set bits 2 and 1 to 0 then we should flash the slowest we possible could. Lets try poking that value: poke $D010, 1 You should now see the cursor flash every 1 second. Lets turn the flashing off just for fun (we can always reset the unit to go back to default). poke $D010, 9 Now the cursor won't flash at all and should be stuck on the on position. This is the because we set the value of 8 (bit 3) + enable (bit 1) = 9 (00001001). But what about bigger numbers? So this is all cool poking and peeking one byte numbers and all, but what about when we need to do something larger? Well fortunately for us in SuperBasic we have a few extra commands that help with this. Command Bytes Max Value peek / poke 1 255 ($FF) peekw / pokew 2 65535 ($FFFF) peekl / pokel 3 16777215 ($FFFFFF) peekd / poked 4 Ridiculously Large Number ($FFFFFF) You might ask why we'd need all these? Especially the larger ones. Well it turns out that 3 and 4 byte numbers are used in colors frequently. For instance, the Foenix keeps its colors in look up tables (or LUTs for short). Each color is assigned a number or index and is comprised of 3 bytes the same as you are probably used to if you ever do any web development. For instance the hex code #641e16 is a dark red. It's made up of three bytes each one representing a value between 0 and 255. The first byte is the amount of red, the second is the amount of blue and the third is the amount of green. When all three are put together it represents a number between 0 and 16777215. Lets do something with that color to demonstrate the point. Enter the following into the basic prompt: poke 1,0 pokel $D848, $641E16 What happened? If you machine behaved like mine, it changed the background to a dark rich red represented by the hex code. This code by the way was just an arbitrary one I picked from htmlcolorcodes.com, but it demontrates why we need pokel as a command. Reset your machine and try this one: poke 1,0 poke $D848, $641E16 Notice it isn't the same color. Thats because the POKE only really changed to the value $16 at the end of that hex code. If you were to use a pokew only the $1E16 would work. So color when it comes to bitmaps and sprites have one more byte attached to them (though at time of writing I'm not sure its used). It's an alpha value. So the format in hex would be RRGGBBAA where A is the alpha value between 0 and 255. This would require a peekd to set. Indirection Operators The commands peek and peekw have a really cool indirection operator shortcut for them as well and it can be confusing if you are coming from other versions of Basic. In Commodore 64 basic the ? is used as a shortcut for print. So the command: ? "Hi" would print hi to the screen. If you tried that on your SuperBasic prompt on the Foenix you'll get the dreaded Type mismatch error. In our world the ? is an indrection operator for both peek and poke. It can be either depending on how it's used. For instance, in the previous examples were we always setting the MMU page to a value before we started poking on things like this: poke 1,0 print peek(1) This will set memory address $0001 to 0 and then print what we set it to. The same commands using the indirection operator would be: ?1 = 0 print ?1 When we use the indirection on the left side of the equals is means set memory address $0001 to 1. Later when we ask it to print ?1 it will do the same thing as printing the peek of memory address $0001. If we use this on our previous cursor example we could go like: ?$D010=1 To make the cursor flash slow or ?$D010=9 To freeze it. Likewise we do have an indirection operator for two byte values as well and its the ! . If we needed to set two bytes in memory and then retrieve it we could just do something like: !$2000=$FFFF print !$2000 Notice the value is 65535, this is the max two bytes can be. At the time of writing there is no indirections for 3 or 4 byte values which is a shame but using poke and peek is pretty common in code. The indirection, while cool, isn't really as readible as it's counterparts. Fun Example This fun example shows a fun way to use pokel. Don't worry too much about the event command, we'll cover it later, just know that this is going to make something happen every 1 second (or 70 frames). 10 event1=0 20 poke 1,0 30 repeat 40 if event(event1, 70) 50 r=random(255):g=random(255):b=random(255) 60 v=r*b*g 70 pokel $D848, v 80 print str$(v)+" "; 90 endif 100 until false If this runs correctly you should see your text screen change color every second and the 3 byte value it was set to be printed onto the screen.

docs.text: SuperBasic vs Other Basics So what is SuperBasic and why did we need our own manual on it? If we follow the wikipedia rabbit hole we'd find that SuperBasic was an improvement on Basic by the folks at Sinclair. I think the idea was to showcase it as the primary basic for a product called the SuperSpectrum, but it never came to fruition. It has however, shown up today in the Foenix series of 8-bit computers were it really shines with the extra memory and modern components inside. Graphics and Text Improvements Commodore basic was a very limited command set and really required the user to do a lot of peeking and poking (see our chapter on that) to get anything accomplished graphically. Superbasic gives direct access to graphics, sprites, text placement, bitmaps and tilesets without the need for direct memory manipulation, though you certainly could do it that way. Example, put text of the screen at a certain position the C64 way: The SuperBasic Way Control Structures IF Then Else Procedures Writing without GOTOS/GOSUBS String Splitting / Parsing LEFT MID RIGHT GETITEM GETITEMCOUNT Timer / Events timer() event()
